name: Four ways to diagnose an ego state
oneLine: Berne's four checks on an ego-state call - behavioural, social, historical, phenomenological - used together, with behavioural doing most of the work and the other three confirming it.
whatYouDid: You needed Noah's hunched apology (behavioural), his coworkers' reflexive reassurance (social), his memory of being called out in school (historical), and his own "back in Mrs Carrow's class" (phenomenological) to all line up before you could call it Child with confidence.
confusion: People diagnose from words alone - what someone said - and stop there; the tell is that behavioural diagnosis is Berne's first and most important check precisely because tone, posture and gesture carry information that content doesn't, and the other three diagnoses exist specifically to verify a call that content alone can't settle.

fromBook.quote: Behavioral diagnosis is the most important of the four. The other three act as checks upon it.

expand.definition: Behavioural (observing words, tones, gestures, postures, expressions), social (how others' ego states respond to you), historical (what you recall of childhood and parents), and phenomenological (actually re-experiencing the ego-state, not just remembering it) - a full diagnosis ideally uses all four, in that order.
expand.otherFraming: Outside therapy, you'll usually only have behavioural and maybe social diagnosis available - that's fine; the practical standard is getting two or more independent checks to agree, not running all four every time.
expand.tryThisToday: Next time you're guessing someone's ego state, ask yourself what ego state you feel pulled to answer from - that pull (social diagnosis) is often your best free second data point.
